items.text: Under MCL 500.2833(1)(m), who may demand appraisal and when?
Either party (insured or insurer) may make a written demand that the amount of loss or actual cash value be set by appraisal once they fail to agree on the actual cash value or amount of the loss.
How many days does each side have to name its appraiser after receiving a written appraisal demand?
20 days after receipt of the written demand.
After the two party appraisers are named, how many days do they have to agree on an umpire before either party can go to court?
15 days. If the two appraisers cannot agree on an umpire within 15 days, either the insured or insurer may ask a judge to select one.
If the appraisers cannot agree on an umpire in 15 days, which court appoints one?
A judge of the circuit court for the county where the loss occurred or where the property is located.
How many of the three (two appraisers plus umpire) must sign to set a binding amount of loss?
Any 2 of the 3. A written agreement signed by any two of the two appraisers and the umpire sets the amount of the loss.
Under MCL 500.2833(1)(m), who pays each party appraiser, and who pays the umpire?
Each appraiser is paid by the party that selected them. The umpire's compensation and other expenses of the appraisal are split equally between the insured and the insurer.
What must the appraisers determine, and at what level of detail, under MCL 500.2833(1)(m)?
The appraisers set the amount of the loss and actual cash value 'as to each item,' meaning a line-item basis, not a single lump-sum figure.
TRAP: How many days does Michigan's appraisal statute give the two appraisers to agree on the amount of loss before submitting differences to the umpire?
The statute does not set a number. It only says 'if the appraisers fail to agree within a reasonable time,' and no Michigan case defines what that reasonable time is.
A homeowner and an insurer disagree only on the dollar amount of hail damage to a roof; coverage for the hailstorm itself is not disputed. What is the correct next step under MCL 500.2833(1)(m)?
Either party may make a written demand for appraisal, since coverage is not in dispute and the disagreement is only about the amount of loss.
A carrier receives a written appraisal demand on March 1 and never responds. By what date must it name its own appraiser, and what can the insured do if it misses that date?

The carrier must name its appraiser by March 21 (20 days after receipt). If it refuses to participate, the insured can ask the circuit court to compel appraisal; that is what the trial court did in Cantina Enterprises II Inc v Property-Owners Ins Co, 349 Mich App 682 (2024), and the Court of Appeals affirmed.
What is the leading Michigan case holding that appraisal decides the amount of loss, not coverage, and how has the Court of Appeals described the process itself?

Auto-Owners Ins Co v Kwaiser, 190 Mich App 482 (1991), published. The court called appraisal 'a simple and inexpensive method for the prompt adjustment and settlement of claims' and a substitute for judicial determination of the amount of a loss.
Per Kwaiser, what must a court do first if the parties cannot agree on coverage at all?
The court must determine coverage in a declaratory action before any appraisal of the damage to the property.
Once an insurer admits a loss is covered, is a court free to deny a motion to compel appraisal?
No. Once an insurer admits that a loss is covered under its policy, a court is statutorily mandated to order the parties to participate in Michigan's statutory appraisal process.

What Michigan Supreme Court case states that 'matters of coverage under an insurance agreement are generally determined by the courts, the method of determining the loss is a matter reserved for the appraisers'?
Dupree v Auto-Owners Ins Co, 497 Mich 1 (2014).
What did Cantina Enterprises II Inc v Property-Owners Ins Co (2024) hold about a carrier that keeps requesting more proof and makes partial payments, but never issues a formal denial?
By making payments on the claim and never formally denying liability, the carrier admitted the loss was covered; the only remaining dispute was the amount owed, which is an appraisal question.
Is Cantina Enterprises II Inc v Property-Owners Ins Co a published or unpublished Court of Appeals opinion, and what is its cite?
Published. 349 Mich App 682; 28 NW3d 800 (2024).
In Cantina, the insured did not submit a signed sworn proof of loss until months after the policy's 60-day deadline. Why did the Court of Appeals still allow the claim to proceed to appraisal?
The carrier waived the 60-day proof-of-loss deadline by continuing to accept documentation and extending its own document requests twice after that deadline had passed.
What did the rescinded-then-clarified OFIS bulletins quoted in Cantina say about a carrier's duty once it admits coverage but disputes scope?

Once an insurer determines a loss is covered and a party demands appraisal, disagreements over whether some claimed damages are part of the amount of loss are part of the appraisal process, not a coverage question for the courts, and the insurer's participation in appraisal is mandatory.
What did Maksym v Auto-Owners Ins Co (COA, published Feb 24, 2026) hold about paying for accepted items while expressly denying others?

Paying for specific items the carrier determined were covered, while expressly disputing liability for other items, is not a 'partial payment' that admits coverage on the disputed items; the insured is not entitled to appraisal on those disputed items.
How did the Maksym court characterize the insureds' reading of Cantina as entitling them to appraisal on their whole $135,000 claim?

The court said it read Cantina's holding to be 'far narrower' than the insureds argued, and that their argument relied on a strained reading that conflates disputes over coverage with the valuation of a claim after liability is acknowledged.

A carrier pays for kitchen ceiling damage it agrees was caused by a pipe leak but writes, 'we deny coverage for the second-floor bathroom and the plumbing repairs themselves.' Under Maksym, can the insured demand appraisal on the bathroom and plumbing items?

No, not on those expressly denied items. Whether they are covered at all remains a disputed coverage question for a court, not an appraisal question, unless and until the carrier admits coverage on them.
Is Maksym v Auto-Owners Ins Co a published opinion, and what Wayne Circuit Court docket number and Court of Appeals number does it carry?
Yes, marked FOR PUBLICATION February 24, 2026. Court of Appeals No. 372827; Wayne Circuit Court LC No. 23-013880-CK.
What is the Michigan standard for what counts as a 'formal denial' of liability that ends the (1)(q) tolling period?

A formal denial must be explicit and unequivocally impress upon the insured the need to pursue further relief in court, per Smitham v State Farm Fire & Cas Co, 297 Mich App 537, 545 (2012), applied in Maksym.

A carrier's letter tells the insured that coverage for certain items 'may be jeopardized' if more documentation is not provided, but does not say those items are denied. Does this letter formally deny liability and start the suit clock running on those items?

No. Language asking for more proof and warning coverage 'may be jeopardized' is not explicit and unequivocal, so under Smitham and Maksym it does not end tolling on those items. Smitham adds the flip side: to end tolling after a partial payment, the insurer must explicitly indicate it is denying all liability in excess of what it has paid.

In Maksym, one letter both expressly denied the plumbing-repair claim AND merely requested more documentation on the second-floor bathroom claim. Can a single letter formally deny some items while leaving others open?

Yes. The Court of Appeals held the plumbing denial was clear and formal, but found a question of fact on whether the bathroom-item language was an equivocal, non-final denial; a single letter can do both.
What case first established, as a matter of Michigan common law, that a suit-limitation clock in an insurance policy is tolled from notice of loss until formal denial of liability?
Tom Thomas Organization, Inc v Reliance Ins Co, 396 Mich 588 (1976), Michigan Supreme Court.
Quote the Michigan Supreme Court's core holding in Tom Thomas Organization v Reliance Ins Co on tolling.

'The appropriate resolution is not to allow the contractual period of limitation to run from the date of the casualty ... but to toll the running of the limitation from the time the insured gives notice until the insurer formally denies liability.'
Was the Tom Thomas tolling rule the court's own invention, or was it later written into the Insurance Code, and when?
It began as judge-made common law in 1976. The Legislature later wrote a tolling rule into MCL 500.2833 when it added that section to the Insurance Code by 1990 PA 305.

In Tom Thomas, the insured gave notice of loss around January 20, 1972 and the insurer denied liability on June 22, 1972. Suit was filed March 16, 1973, more than 12 months after the December 14, 1971 loss date. Why was the suit timely?
The 12-month clock was tolled for about 5 months, from notice until formal denial, so the deadline did not expire until roughly mid-May 1973; the March 1973 filing came before that.
What did Rory v Continental Ins Co, 473 Mich 457 (2005), hold about enforcing a clear, one-year contractual limitation period?
A court must construe and apply unambiguous contract provisions as written; a judicial assessment that the provision is merely 'unreasonable' is not a valid basis to refuse to enforce it.
Under Rory, what CAN get a Michigan court to refuse to enforce a clear, unambiguous limitation-period clause?
Only that the provision violates law or public policy, or that a traditional contract defense (such as fraud or duress) applies. A judge's personal sense of unfairness is not enough.
An insured argues a policy's one-year suit deadline is simply too short to be fair and asks a court to extend it. Under Rory, how should a Michigan court rule?
The court should enforce the one-year deadline as written; 'too short to be fair' is a reasonableness argument, which Rory says is not a valid basis to override a clear contract term.
May a policyholder's party appraiser under MCL 500.2833(1)(m) be paid on a contingency-fee basis in Michigan?
Yes. White v State Farm Fire & Cas Co, 293 Mich App 419 (2011), holds a contingency-fee agreement does not disqualify a party appraiser from being 'independent' as the statute requires.
What disclosure does White v State Farm require when a party appraiser has a contingency-fee arrangement?
The opposing party must be made aware that a contingency-fee agreement exists.
MCL 500.2833(1)(m) uses two different adjectives for the two party appraisers versus the umpire. What are they, and why does White v State Farm say that distinction matters?

Party appraisers must be 'competent, independent'; the umpire must be 'competent, impartial.' White reasons that only the umpire must be neutral to both sides; a party appraiser may act as an advocate for the side that selected them, similar to an attorney.

A homeowner hires a public adjuster on a 10% contingency fee and names that adjuster as the party appraiser in an appraisal demand, without mentioning the fee to the carrier. Is this a problem under White?

Yes. The contingency fee itself does not disqualify the appraiser, but White requires the opposing party (the carrier) be made aware the contingency-fee agreement exists; failing to disclose it is the exposure, not the fee arrangement itself.
Under Dupree v Auto-Owners Ins Co, 497 Mich 1 (2014), on what grounds can a Michigan court set aside a signed appraisal award?
Judicial review of appraisal awards is limited to instances of bad faith, fraud, misconduct, or manifest mistake.
In Dupree, the appraisal award set actual cash value at $128,250.12 and calculated depreciation of $39,673.48. Was the insured automatically entitled to the depreciation amount too?

No. The Supreme Court held the ACV award alone did not entitle her to the withheld depreciation; she still had to satisfy the policy's replacement-cost condition by proving she actually repaired or replaced the property.
A signed appraisal award sets a hail-damage roof loss at $18,000. The carrier says it simply disagrees with how the appraisers valued the shingles. Can it get the award set aside?

No. Under Dupree, judicial review of an appraisal award is limited to bad faith, fraud, misconduct, or manifest mistake, and plain disagreement with the appraisers' valuation judgment is none of those. No Michigan case verified here defines 'manifest mistake' any further, so do not assume an ordinary error qualifies.
MCL 500.2833(1)(q) sets the suit-limitation period at what length, and what is the trap in how that length is phrased?
1 year after the loss, OR the time period specified in the policy, whichever is longer. The trap: it is not always exactly 1 year; a policy that grants more time controls.
Quote MCL 500.2833(1)(q)'s tolling sentence verbatim.
'The time for commencing an action is tolled from the time the insured notifies the insurer of the loss until the insurer formally denies liability.'
MCL 500.2833(1)(p) sets what payment deadline once amount of loss is proven, and what section is it subject to?
The loss is payable within 30 days after receipt of proof of amount of loss, except as otherwise provided in MCL 500.2845 (the fire loss withholding section).
When was MCL 500.2833, the section containing the modern appraisal and suit-limit provisions, added to the Michigan Insurance Code?
By 1990 PA 305, effective immediately, December 14, 1990, fourteen years after the judge-made Tom Thomas tolling rule.
A homeowner's policy states a suit must be filed within 18 months of loss, longer than the statutory 1-year floor. Which controls?
The 18-month policy period controls, because MCL 500.2833(1)(q) sets the deadline at 1 year or the time period specified in the policy, whichever is longer.
A Michigan fire policy says the suit clock is tolled only 'in the event we formally deny liability.' Is that condition enforceable?

No. Smitham v State Farm Fire & Cas Co, 297 Mich App 537 (2012), held that policy language conditioning tolling on a formal denial conflicts with MCL 500.2833(1)(q), which contains no such condition, so the policy language is absolutely void under MCL 500.2860. Tolling runs from notice whether or not a formal denial ever comes.

A carrier keeps extending its own document-request deadlines and continues to accept proof-of-loss materials well past the policy's stated proof-of-loss deadline. What did Cantina say this does to the carrier's ability to later claim the proof of loss was untimely?
The carrier waives that timeliness defense; communicating that it will continue to accept the statement of loss past the contractual deadline is an express waiver of the deadline.
Where does an insured go to compel a circuit court to appoint an umpire when the two party appraisers cannot agree within 15 days?
The circuit court for the county in which the loss occurred or in which the property is located.
What happens to the insured's claim if the two appraisers, acting alone without the umpire, submit a written report of agreement to the insurer?
That agreed amount becomes the amount of the loss; the umpire is only brought in if the two appraisers fail to agree within a reasonable time.

A restoration contractor wants to name itself as the 'independent' appraiser on a job where it is also owed a percentage-based consulting fee tied to the claim outcome. Does White v State Farm license this arrangement?

No. White addressed a licensed appraiser's own contingency-fee compensation with disclosure; it does not authorize a contractor with an unrelated financial stake in the outcome to appoint itself appraiser, which raises separate independence and unlicensed-adjusting concerns.

Name the case establishing that appraisal is 'a substitute for judicial determination of a dispute concerning the amount of a loss' and its purpose is 'to resolve the amount of loss in insurance disputes where liability has been admitted.'
Auto-Owners Ins Co v Kwaiser, 190 Mich App 482, 486-487 (1991), as quoted in Cantina Enterprises II Inc v Property-Owners Ins Co, 349 Mich App 682, 693 (2024).

A carrier's adjuster inspects storm damage and confirms in writing that the storm is a covered event, then disputes only whether the insured's claimed number of damaged shingle squares is accurate. Is this a coverage dispute or an amount-of-loss dispute?
An amount-of-loss (scope) dispute. Coverage for the storm is admitted; the disagreement over quantity/extent of damage is exactly the kind of factual dispute Michigan courts send to appraisal.
What Sixth Circuit case, though only persuasive (unpublished federal), summarized the Michigan rule that a court must decide coverage first if liability is not admitted?
The D Boys, LLC v Mid-Century Ins Co, 644 Fed Appx 574 (6th Cir 2016).
Did Rory v Continental Ins Co (2005) wipe out the Tom Thomas tolling rule?

No. Rory overruled Tom Thomas and Camelot only 'to the degree that [they] abrogate unambiguous contractual terms on the basis of reasonableness determinations.' Rory itself pointed out that the Tom Thomas holding rested on judicial tolling, not on reasonableness, and that the Tom Thomas majority expressly declined to decide whether a one-year limit was reasonable. For fire policies the tolling rule now sits in MCL 500.2833(1)(q) anyway.

A Michigan insured wants to argue that her one-year suit deadline should be extended because she did not understand the policy language. Under Rory, is 'I did not understand it' a valid basis to avoid the deadline?

No. Rory limits challenges to unambiguous provisions to traditional contract defenses (fraud, duress, and similar); a claim of personal misunderstanding of clear language is not one of those defenses.
What must the two party appraisers do under MCL 500.2833(1)(m) if they cannot agree on the amount of loss?
They must submit their differences to the umpire.

A homeowner's roof claim: the carrier's adjuster inspects, confirms hail is a covered peril, and pays for a single 'test square' patch on one slope. The contractor documents hail hits on all four slopes and requests full replacement; the carrier refuses the additional scope but never says the other slopes were not damaged by hail. Is this file on the appraisal track or the coverage-fight track?
The appraisal track. Coverage for the hail event is admitted; the dispute is purely the extent (scope/amount) of covered damage, which Michigan law sends to appraisal, not to a coverage lawsuit.

Same hail-roof file, but this time the carrier's letter says explicitly, 'the north slope shows only pre-existing wear, not hail impact, and that portion of the claim is denied.' What must the homeowner do with the north slope before demanding appraisal on the rest?

Carve the north-slope item out of the appraisal demand; that item is now a coverage dispute (was it caused by the covered peril at all) and needs a separate resolution path (settlement, carve-out, or litigation), per the Maksym rule.
What did the December 2017 OFIS memorandum clarify about the 2017 rescission of Bulletin 2006-07-INS?

The rescission did not mean insurers could refuse to submit to appraisal when liability is not disputed; the Director continued to consider participation in appraisal under (1)(m) mandatory in those situations.

An insured's proof of loss claims $135,000 including several items marked 'to be determined' with no supporting documentation. The carrier rejects those specific line items for lack of proof but does not say they are not covered. Is a demand for appraisal on the undocumented 'to be determined' items likely to succeed?

The exact wording of the carrier's letter controls. In Cantina the carrier called the proofs insufficient while still paying on the claim and inviting more proof, and the insured got appraisal. In Maksym the carrier rejected the unproven items and then wrote that it was 'unable to consider the additional scope,' which the Court of Appeals treated as a formal denial of liability on those items, so no appraisal was available on them while coverage stayed in dispute.
What must an insured do before an action under the fire insurance policy may even be commenced, per MCL 500.2833(1)(q)?
Comply with the policy's requirements; an action under the policy may be commenced only after compliance with the policy requirements.
